opening_summary: Thirty-two terms for making a short film that sells a game you built, from the hook to the call to action. Knowing the exact term lets you tell an editor, or an AI coding agent, precisely what to change.
opening_description: 32 terms for making a trailer for your game.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often think a trailer shows the game they plan to make. It does not. A trailer shows real play from the build you have, builds to one peak, and ends on one action. A planned feature on screen is a promise you cannot keep. This film goes through the terms of making a trailer, each one shown.
idea.text:
A trailer shows
the game you plan to make.
idea.triggerWords: the game you plan to make

beats.narration: This table is the map. Thirty-two terms for a short film that sells a game, in four groups. The first group is what you are making. Trailer, teaser, gameplay video, pitch film, pitch, logline, tagline, hook, key art and thumbnail. The kind of film, and the idea it sells.

The second group is shape and length. Beat structure, climax, title card, call to action, logo sting, runtime, frame rate and resolution. These terms say where each part of the film goes, and how long it runs.

The third group is cutting and sound. Pacing, cut on action, BPM, which means beats per minute, cut on the beat, music drop, sound design and muted test. These terms say how the cuts and the music work together.

The fourth group is capture and honesty. Fixed frame rate, Movie Maker mode, clean footage, gameplay vs cinematic, honest trailer, viewer test and accessibility. These terms cover getting real footage of your game, and keeping the promise the film makes.

A chart of film lengths, from zero to six hundred seconds. A Trailer is a short film that sells a game to a stranger, someone who owes you nothing. It shows the best real moments and ends on one action. Store trailers run thirty to ninety seconds, the top bar. For example, you cut together the best moments of your platformer, the jump, the spikes, the goal flag, and end on one line that says where to play it.

A Teaser is an early look that hints at a game and shows little. It announces the game and saves the rest for later. Its bar is the short one, fifteen to forty-five seconds, and that range is made up for this example. A trailer sells, and a teaser only hints. For example, before your game has a finished level, you post a short clip of the hero's silhouette and one jump, then the title, and nothing more.

A Gameplay video is plain footage of play, made to cover the game, not to sell it. It shows play as it is and makes no argument. Its bar is the long one, three to ten minutes, a range that is also made up. For example, you record yourself playing the first level of your game from start to finish, with no cuts and no music, so a reviewer can see exactly how it plays.

A Pitch film argues for a project. It tells a reviewer what you will build and why, and in this course it runs two to four minutes, the red bar. It is about a project, not a finished game for sale. For example, you show captured play of the one room your game has today, then say what the final project will add, labelling what exists and what will exist.

A block of text with a red bar for its length, for a made-up game called Tilt. A Pitch is a short sales description of the game idea, a few sentences long. This one is thirty-two words. It says what the game is, what is new, and how long a level takes. For example, the few sentences at the top of your game design document, telling a classmate why your platformer is worth playing, are its pitch.

A second, shorter block and bar. A Logline is the game in one sentence, who does what, and what is new. Here the pitch is cut from thirty-two words to thirteen. A platformer where you reverse gravity to turn every hazard into a pathway. For example, if your game is a platformer where the player swaps places with their own shadow to cross gaps, that one sentence, the kind you would say to a recruiter, is its logline.

A Tagline is a few memorable words that sit beside the title. Fall up is only two words. It cannot explain the game, it can only be remembered. A logline explains, and a tagline does not. For example, under the title on your game's poster you might print the words, one more jump. Nobody could work out how the game plays from them, and that is fine for a tagline.

A drawing that builds one sentence from a mechanic. The Hook is the most distinctive thing the player does, said in one sentence. It names what you do and what that changes. Here, you reverse gravity to turn hazards into pathways, eight words. A tagline is memorable words, and a hook is the one thing nobody else has. For example, if the player in your game can freeze an enemy and stand on it, the hook is, freeze an enemy to make your next step.

Two openings on a timeline, with a red line at five seconds. The hook test asks for gameplay in the first five seconds. In this made-up example, the first opening, A, spends that time on black and a studio logo, so play starts at six seconds, and it fails. Opening B starts on play and passes. For example, open the trailer for your platformer on the player already in the air over the spikes, not on your team's name.
figures: A: first play at 6.0 s, fails the 5 s test

beats.narration: A poster. Key art is the one still image that stands for the game, with a title, one character and one idea. Here the title Tilt, a single block for the character, a red triangle pointing the other way for gravity flipped, and the tagline at the bottom. For example, for your platformer you might draw the hero leaping over a pit of spikes, with the title above, as the one image on the game's store page.

The same poster at three sizes. A Thumbnail is the small preview image, the key art at store size, and it has to read at a glance. The title shrinks with the image. At three hundred pixels wide it reads. At forty-five pixels wide it is too small, by a made-up threshold of twelve pixels. For example, shrink your game's poster to the size of a store tile, and check that the title can still be made out.

A timeline of the Shipping Lane trailer, thirty point five seconds long. Beat structure is the order of a trailer's parts. Hook, establish, escalate, peak, title, button, call to action. Each part has a length, and the lengths add up to the runtime. For example, in a trailer for your platformer, the hook is one striking jump, establish shows the controls, escalate adds enemies, and the peak is the last run to the goal.

Now the peak is lit in red. The Climax, or peak, is the biggest payoff, placed on a strong beat of the music after a quiet drop. Here the music drops from nineteen to twenty seconds, and the peak starts at twenty seconds. That is beat forty, exactly ten bars of four, a downbeat. For example, in your trailer, the moment the player clears the last spike and lands beside the goal flag can be the climax.

A Title card is a held card with the game's name, and it comes after the peak, not at the start. Here it holds for one and a half seconds, forty-five frames at thirty frames per second. The name of a game nobody knows is the least interesting way to open. For example, right after your player lands the final jump, cut to your game's name in large letters on a plain card.

Bars on an axis from zero to one hundred twenty seconds. Runtime is how long the film runs. A store trailer is typically thirty to ninety seconds, and sixty to ninety is a good first target. The trailer gate, an automatic check, accepts fifteen to one hundred twenty. Shipping Lane runs thirty point five. For example, if your trailer shows the same jump in three shots, cutting two of them shortens the runtime without losing anything.

Two rows of ticks, one second of film each. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. Frames are frame rate times seconds, so the thirty point five second film is nine hundred fifteen frames at thirty, and one thousand eight hundred thirty at sixty. For example, if your game is captured at sixty frames per second, every second of the player's run is stored as twice as many pictures as at thirty.

A small grey frame inside a large pink one. Resolution is the width and height of each frame in pixels. 4K has four times the pixels of 1080p, so it needs a stronger machine to capture. Frame rate is images per second, and resolution is pixels per image. For example, the trailer gate wants native 4K footage, so you run your game at that full size while you capture it, not in a small window.

Nine shots before the title, with lengths from the Shipping Lane shot list. Pacing is how fast the cuts come, counted in cuts per minute. It rises toward the peak, but only after the viewer understands the game. Here it goes from twenty, to twenty-five point seven, to thirty. For example, you hold the first shots of your platformer long enough to show the controls, then cut faster as the enemies pile up before the final jump.

A jump arc, simulated with made-up inputs. Cut on action means cutting while a motion is under way, so the eye carries across the cut. Before the jump, at A, the speed is zero. At the top, B, it is twenty-four pixels a frame. Two frames after takeoff, at C, it is forty-one. Cut at C. For example, cut just after your player leaves the ground, and open the next shot with the player still rising.

Three rows of beat ticks over four seconds. BPM, beats per minute, is the tempo of the music. Sixty divided by it gives the seconds between beats. At ninety BPM a beat comes every zero point six six seven seconds. At one hundred twenty, every half second. At one hundred forty, every zero point four two nine. For example, you check the music you picked for your trailer, find it is one hundred twenty BPM, and know a beat falls every half second.

Rough cuts on top, a beat grid at one hundred twenty BPM, and snapped cuts below. Cut on the beat means placing each cut on a beat of the music, so picture and sound lock together. In this made-up example, five of nine cuts started near a beat, and after snapping all nine are. For example, the cut from your title screen to the first jump moves a few frames later, so it lands exactly on a drum hit.

Bars for the loudness of the Shipping Lane music, from its own measurements. A Music drop is a quiet moment just before the peak, so the peak lands. The build is zero point one four, the drop zero point zero one six, about eighteen point eight decibels quieter, then the peak at zero point one seven. For example, the music in your trailer falls almost silent while your player hangs over the final gap, then returns as they land.

A line for the music's loudness over three seconds. Sound design is how you mix, so the music sets the tone and the game's own hits punch through. At each hit the music steps down six decibels, then recovers. That depth is made up for this example. For example, when your player stomps an enemy, the stomp sound comes through clearly while the music dips under it for a moment.

Seven voice lines from the Shipping Lane shot list, each with a tick. The Muted test checks that the film still makes sense with the sound off. Every voice line is also shown on screen, so zero of seven are lost. Sound design is about the mix, and the muted test is about no sound at all. For example, you watch your trailer on mute, and if the voice says press Space to jump, the screen shows it too.
figures: Lost with the sound off: 0 of 7 lines

beats.narration: Two strips of bright frames, and a caption box. Accessibility means more people can watch the film, with captions for speech and no rapid flashing. A common limit is no more than three flashes in any second. In this made-up example, the first sequence, A, has four in its worst second, too many, and sequence B has two. For example, if your trailer flashes the screen white on every explosion, count the flashes before you cut, and caption every spoken line.

The end card of the Shipping Lane trailer, its last five point five seconds. A Call to action is one thing to do next, wishlist, play, or follow a link. Here it is one button, download on GitHub, held for one hundred sixty-five frames, eighteen percent of the runtime. One action, not four social handles, and no fade to black. For example, end your trailer on your game's title and one line, play it in the browser, held long enough to read.

Two openings over the first ten seconds. A Logo sting is a very short logo animation with a sound, and it belongs at the end. Put first, it leaves seven seconds of play instead of ten, so in this made-up example the viewer sees thirty percent less play before deciding. A call to action asks for something, and a sting only signs the work. For example, play your team's short animated logo with its chime after the end card, never before the first jump.

Two rows of frames, three seconds of play on a slow machine. A Fixed frame rate locks rendering to a set number of frames a second, so every frame is the same slice of game time and runs match. Each frame here takes a made-up fifty milliseconds to draw. In real time, sixty frames reach the file. Fixed at sixty, all one hundred eighty do. For example, a command-line test of your game at a fixed sixty frames a second gives the same result on any laptop.

A command typed in a terminal. Movie Maker mode is Godot's mode that records a run to a video file, frame by frame, at the rate you fix. The write movie flag names the file, the fixed frames per second flag sets sixty, and quit after stops at one thousand eight hundred frames, thirty seconds of play. For example, to capture your platformer's first level for a trailer, you run it with these flags and get a smooth video file even on a slow laptop.

One captured frame from a game. Clean footage is real play with the debug clutter hidden, and any HUD, the heads-up display, kept where it explains a mechanic. Here the frames per second counter, the collider overlay and a debug print are hidden, three of five items, while the token counter and the retries stay. For example, before you record your game, turn off the collision shapes you showed for testing, but keep the coin counter.

A list of what trailer footage may be. Gameplay vs cinematic is the rule that footage is captured play from the real build, and a cinematic is allowed only if it is the game's own and is labelled. A rehearsed input route and the best of several takes are allowed. Teleporting, invincibility and mock-up footage are not. For example, the cutscene your game really plays at the end of a level may appear, labelled, but a fly-through rendered outside the game may not.

A feature list, made up for this example. An Honest trailer shows only what the game really does, and planned features never appear. Here jump, bump block, shield and stomp are implemented and may appear. Checkpoints are only planned, so they never do. Four of five. A trailer is a promise, and the game has to keep it. For example, if your double jump works only in a test scene and not in the build, leave it out.

A plan for two viewers, with results still pending. The Viewer test means showing the cut, unexplained, to someone new, stopping at ten seconds, and asking what kind of game it is and what the player does. One viewer watches with sound, one without. You already know the game, so you cannot judge the cut yourself. Nobody has run this test yet. For example, show your trailer to a classmate who has never played your game, and where their attention drifts, cut.

Each pair sets look-alike terms side by side. A Trailer sells the game and shows enough to convince, here twelve shots in sixty seconds, ending on one action. A Teaser announces it and saves the rest, three shots in twenty seconds, ending on a hint.

A Logline is one sentence that explains the game, here thirteen words. A Tagline is a few words to remember, and it explains nothing. Fall up is two words. Ask whether a stranger could tell how the game plays from it.

Cut on action cuts while the motion is moving. At point C the jump moves forty-one pixels a frame, and at point A, zero. Cut on the beat cuts when the music pulses. A rough cut at five point eight seven seconds snaps to six.

Key art is the full still image that stands for the game, with a title sixty-four pixels tall. A Thumbnail is the same art at store size, where that title shrinks to about twenty-six pixels. Same picture, smaller, and it still has to read.

Vague requests on the left, exact instructions under them, and what each one does on the right. Make the trailer shorter becomes, cut it from ninety seconds to sixty, one thousand eight hundred frames at thirty frames per second. That is nine hundred fewer frames, a third less.

Make it more exciting becomes, shorten shots from three seconds to one and a half toward the peak, after the game is shown. That doubles the pace, from twenty to forty cuts a minute. The floor for a shot is zero point eight seconds.

Put it on the music becomes, at one hundred twenty BPM, move every cut to the nearest half-second beat. Cuts that were up to one hundred seventy milliseconds off the beat end at zero, with nine cuts on the grid.

Start strong becomes, show gameplay by five seconds, and put the logo last. With the logo first, play starts at six seconds, which misses the limit by one second. With gameplay first, play starts at zero.

Tell them what to do becomes, end on one action, held five point five seconds, with the title, the platform and one link. In a thirty point five second film that is eighteen percent of the runtime, one hundred sixty-five frames. Long enough to read, short enough to keep.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before a trailer goes out. First, does real gameplay show in the first five seconds? If a logo or a fade comes first, move it to the end.
Second, can you say the hook in one sentence, what the player does and what that changes? If you cannot, the trailer cannot find it either, and the problem is in the design.
Third, is every shot readable, and are the cuts on the beat? Hold each shot long enough to follow, then snap each cut to the beat grid of the music.
Fourth, is every shot real play from this build? A rehearsed route and the best of several takes are fine. Mock-ups, invincibility and planned features are not.
Fifth, does it work with the sound off, with no rapid flashing? Run the muted test, then count the flashes in every second of the film.
Sixth, is there one call to action, held long enough to read? Then say it exactly. Not make it exciting, but one and a half second shots into the peak.

recap_lines: A trailer sells a game to a stranger, and a teaser only hints.
A logline explains the game in one sentence, and a tagline is only remembered.
Show real gameplay in the first five seconds, and put the logo last.
The peak lands on a strong beat, right after a quiet music drop.
Cut on action follows the motion, and cut on the beat follows the music.
An honest trailer shows only real play from the build, never planned features.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on trailer terms with short cases about making a trailer for a game I built, one at a time. Use the terms trailer, teaser, logline, tagline, hook, climax, title card, call to action, cut on action and cut on the beat. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply.
checks: Check: each case is about a game trailer, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 1 (map) puts accessibility in the group 'Capture and honesty', but its entry is on slide 9 under the eyebrow 'Cutting and sound'.
Slide 10 (Call to action and logo sting) carries the eyebrow 'Shape and length' but sits after the three 'Cutting and sound' slides (7 to 9), so the groups do not run in the map's order.

Slide 12 step 1 marks 'slow motion or speed-up' as not allowed and cites 'Assignment 8, honesty rule', but Assignment 8 allows 'Scripted-input captures and slowed replays' when they are labelled. The narration does not mention slow motion.

Slide 8 is badged 'Illustrative data', but step 3 is headed 'MEASURED ENERGY (RMS), SHIPPING LANE CUE' and the note says those values are measured, and step 1 is plain arithmetic. Only the rough cut times of step 2 are invented.
Slide 8 step 2: 'The gate fails a cut with under 60% on the beat.' A single cut cannot be 60% on the beat; it presumably means a film whose cuts are under 60% on the beat fails.

Slide 12's TELL THESE APART box is Trailer vs Gameplay video, which contrasts none of that slide's three terms (gameplay vs cinematic, honest trailer, viewer test), and gives Trailer as 'sells; keeps its promise' where slide 2 says 'sells; ends on one action'.

Slide 2 tags Pitch film 'outside source', but the title-slide note defines outside source as the godot-trailer skill or general film vocabulary, and the slide itself says the pitch film comes from Assignment 8.

Slide 5 step 2: '40 ÷ 4 = bar 10 exactly' is ambiguous. With the first beat at 0 s, beat 40 at 20.0 s is the first beat of the eleventh bar (ten bars completed). The narration says 'exactly ten bars of four, a downbeat'.
Slide 9 step 3: the strips are titled 'BRIGHT FRAMES' but the flashes are drawn as dark blocks on a light ground, so a viewer can read the dark blocks as dark frames.
Slide 13 pair 1 gives '12 shots in 60 s' and '3 shots in 20 s' with no source and no illustrative label; the slide's note does not say where the counts come from.
The title slide's note says 'Deck 11 of the topic order'; this is deck 22 in the film set.
